text: Food, as we all know. <break time="0.8s" /> Is essential for human life. <break time="0.8s" /> It also is the basis for several major industries. <break time="0.8s" /> Found in many countries around the world. <break time="0.8s" /> Such as in agriculture, food processing, food retailing and food service. <break time="0.8s" /> For millennia. <break time="0.8s" /> The focus of those involved with food. <break time="0.8s" /> As a human and economic phenomenon. <break time="0.8s" /> Was on its production, preservation, distribution, pricing. <break time="0.8s" /> And other practical concerns. <break time="0.8s" /> But in the late 18th century. <break time="0.8s" /> This began to change. <break time="0.8s" /> Food became more than just a life necessity. <break time="0.8s" /> Restaurants began to be developed. <break time="0.8s" /> Initially in France. <break time="0.8s" /> But eventually in other nations. <break time="0.8s" /> As a distinct institution. <break time="0.8s" /> Offering people dining choices and table service. <break time="0.8s" /> The opportunity for socialization. <break time="0.8s" /> And, over time. <break time="0.8s" /> A finer and finer atmosphere. <break time="0.8s" /> The rise of restaurants eventually led to a class of diners. <break time="0.8s" /> Who prided themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> On being critics of taste, food and cooking. <break time="0.8s" /> Brillat Savarin is probably the best known. <break time="0.8s" /> Of the culinary philosophers. <break time="0.8s" /> Or, in todays parlance, a foodie. <break time="0.8s" /> One of Brillat Savarins better known sayings was tell me what you eat. <break time="0.8s" /> And I will tell you who you are.
